narrative.text: The cover of the Russian edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The title page of the Russian edition of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.
The cataloguing and copyright page of the Russian eHealth strategy toolkit, with WHO and ITU ISBNs, 2012 copyright and standard disclaimers.

The foreword to the eHealth strategy toolkit by the WHO Director-General and the ITU Secretary-General, presenting it as a major result of their collaboration to help countries at any level use ICT in health for measurable benefits. They note it brings together stakeholders in a national effort to advance public and individual health.

Acknowledgements for the eHealth strategy toolkit, naming the WHO and ITU steering committee and technical advisers, Deloitte consultants, editorial and design staff, and the many country and agency reviewers, including from Egypt, Ghana, Mexico and USAID.
The table of contents of the Russian eHealth toolkit, listing the foreword, acknowledgements, introduction and its three parts on vision, action plan and monitoring and evaluation.

Introduces the eHealth strategy toolkit as a practical, step-by-step guide that any government can use to develop or revise a national eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework. It notes that implementation depends on sustained stakeholder engagement and periodic review.

Explains that the eHealth toolkit has three parts building on Part 1: a national vision, an action plan and a monitoring plan. It lists the toolkit's aims, such as better coordination of eHealth activities and defining the strategic context.

Completes the list of toolkit aims, including understanding the existing eHealth environment and setting short-, medium- and long-term goals, and notes that the approach also serves the general public as ultimate beneficiaries.
The title page for Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, on developing a national eHealth vision.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The title page for Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, on developing a national eHealth vision.
A repeat of the cataloguing and copyright page of the Russian eHealth strategy toolkit, with ISBNs and disclaimers.

States the purpose of Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit as a resource for countries starting out or revisiting existing investments in eHealth. It outlines how its chapters cover the national context, organizing the process, stakeholder engagement, and gathering and analysing information to develop a vision and recommendations.

The table of contents for Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, listing twelve chapters from national eHealth context to refining the vision and strategic recommendations, and annexes on examples, benefits, methodology and definitions.
A list of figures and boxes in Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, covering models of the national eHealth vision, governance, stakeholder roles and component maps.
A list of tables in Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, covering eHealth impacts, governance bodies, stakeholder consultation, health system aspects, eHealth components and prioritization factors.

Opens chapter 1 of the eHealth toolkit by making the case for eHealth, defined by WHO as the use of ICT for health, explaining how it is transforming health service delivery and underpins responsive health systems. It cites a WHO Global Observatory for eHealth report.

Notes that WHO and ITU governing bodies have adopted resolutions urging national eHealth strategies, and explains the complementary roles of health and ICT ministries. It describes how shared goals allow coordinated action, citing a World Health Assembly resolution and an Australian strategy definition.

A table of examples of eHealth impacts for citizens, researchers and practitioners, health managers and others, such as personalized care, access to knowledge and remote services. It also introduces the enabling environment for eHealth, including governance, legislation, standards and human resources.

Figure 1 of the Russian edition of a national eHealth strategy toolkit shows three national contexts defined by the ICT environment and the eHealth enabling environment: experimentation and early adoption, development and building, and scale-up. The text begins describing the first context, where scattered projects depend on donors and NGOs and the country cannot meet public health reporting obligations.

Explains that in the early adoption context eHealth is driven by better access and quality, such as telemedicine for remote areas, and that national plans should build the case for investment, skills and priority services. It warns against assuming countries can leapfrog to advanced systems without an enabling environment. It then describes the development context, with wider telemedicine networks, limited electronic records and mobile health pilots.

Says that in the development stage national plans should strengthen the enabling environment, legal frameworks and standards to avoid ever-larger vertical systems. In the scale-up context, the enabling environment catches up with ICT and national action is needed on standards, laws and investment, data use, privacy and monitoring.

Table 2 summarises the three national eHealth contexts, from small unconnected pilot projects dependent on donors to larger projects and eventually scaled-up national systems. It describes typical infrastructure, markets, funding and reporting capacity at each stage. The text after the table explains that the strategy and plan become more detailed and effective at each stage.

Table 3 links each national context to a strategic focus and example actions, such as building awareness and governance early on, then standards and legal certainty, then scale-up. Figure 2 lists the components of eHealth, including leadership and governance, strategy and investment, services and applications, standards, infrastructure, legislation and workforce.

Table 4 divides eHealth components into the enabling environment and the ICT environment and describes the role of each, such as national leadership and coordination, flexible strategy and investment planning, and services and applications for patients, providers and others.

Opens Chapter 2 on the national eHealth vision model, which explains why a national approach is needed, what it will achieve and how. It shows the model's elements and defines the strategic context in terms of population health, health system status, health priorities and development goals.

Explains how detailed health goals identify where ICT investment can improve health and support development, together forming the strategic context. It describes moving from context to an eHealth vision of an enabled health system and notes a suggested structure for the vision document in Annex C.

Chapter 3 outlines the methodology for developing a national eHealth vision, which draws on country experience and requires leadership, a well-managed process and stakeholder engagement. It describes an iterative approach that first drafts an unconstrained vision and then adjusts it to the current environment, leading to recommendations for the implementation plan.

Summarises the methodology steps of defining the strategic context from health and development goals and reviewing trends and other countries' experience. It also covers drafting the vision, identifying required components and assessing the current eHealth environment, including existing assets such as e-government components.

Describes the final methodology steps of analysing opportunities and gaps and refining the vision into strategic recommendations, which feed into the implementation plan and are then approved and shared.

Chapter 4 on managing the process explains that strong leadership and governance improve transparency, trust and coordination in developing a national eHealth vision. It lists required actions and expected outputs, ending with a well-managed process reflecting health priorities and stakeholder needs.

Stresses the need for sustained high-level leadership and a respected champion from the health sector who secures funding and resources. It introduces governance structures, such as health leadership, a steering committee, the strategy team and stakeholder advisory groups.

Table 5 gives examples of governance bodies, their functions and membership, from health sector leaders such as the minister to a steering committee that approves the vision and oversees progress. It notes that coordination needs grow with the size and complexity of the stakeholder landscape.

Describes the core strategy team needed for the project-based approach, which should understand the health system and may draw on other agencies or the private sector. It lists required skills, such as strategic analysis and stakeholder engagement, and notes timelines of 12 to 19 weeks.
Figure 6 shows two example timelines, of about 12 and 19 weeks, for the steps in developing a national eHealth vision.

Chapter 5 on stakeholder engagement explains that a well-researched and supported eHealth vision requires collaboration with stakeholders from different sectors, according to the government's role. It ends with planning and conducting consultations to achieve a vision stakeholders support.

Explains that strategy development varies with the government's role in eHealth, and Table 6 sets out implications for planning from fully regulated to market-led settings. It begins listing health sector stakeholders, such as professional associations, hospitals and research institutes.

Completes the list of health sector stakeholders, including insurers, patient groups, public health bodies, private providers, ICT vendors and media. It also lists stakeholders outside health, such as civil registration services and ICT ministries, and stresses engaging those most affected or influential.

Describes four common stakeholder roles in developing the vision, from decision-makers and key influencers to engaged stakeholders and the wider public. Figure 7 and Table 7 set out their roles, with examples such as advisers, health executives, health workers, families and community groups.

Explains that each stakeholder group needs a tailored engagement approach aligned with a communication plan, noting the media's importance for reaching the public. It recommends that the project team prepare a detailed stakeholder consultation plan.

Table 9 gives an example plan for consulting decision-makers, key influencers, wider stakeholders and the public at each stage of developing the national eHealth vision. Early stages gather input on the strategic context and health system problems, with decision-makers reviewing and approving goals. Later stages run through to presenting the approved vision to the public through awareness and education campaigns.

Advises reducing repeated consultations with the same stakeholders by staging them. Table 10 gives an example approach with questions for early consultations, such as health priorities, the 5–10-year vision and risks, and mechanisms such as interviews and workshops.

Chapter 6 on defining the strategic context explains that it describes priority health system goals that eHealth can help address, based on population health, the health system, health strategy and development goals. It lists actions and expected outputs, including the potential role of eHealth.

Describes studying population health and demographics, with Table 11 posing questions on population size and structure, current health outcomes such as life expectancy and main diseases, and expected changes over 10–20 years. It suggests interviews with planning bodies to understand influences on health.

Describes analysing the health system, with Table 12 posing questions on services, institutional structures, workforce and other aspects. Expected outputs are a summary of the health system, its challenges and priorities, and potential obstacles to eHealth.

Recommends combining desk research, including WHO country reports, with interviews of health sector stakeholders to understand the health system. It then introduces analysis of health strategy, goals and priorities, citing commitments such as the Millennium Development Goals and International Health Regulations.

Explains that the expected output is a set of agreed strategic themes, goals and priorities, which may need consolidating from several national and regional documents through consultation. It also calls for identifying development factors in other sectors relevant to eHealth.

Recommends internal analysis of documents and regional agreements from other ministries, such as Millennium Development Goals or European Commission directives, validated through interviews with senior stakeholders. It then explains how to select strategic goals spanning public health, the health system and wider development.

Table 14 gives example questions for strategic goals in areas such as public health, equity and access, health workforce supply and distribution, and health system structure. It notes these are only examples and actual goals will vary by country, although the process is common.

Describes, in the Russian edition of the national eHealth strategy toolkit, the step of linking health information flows to the strategic goals set earlier, to see how those flows may need to change. It explains that electronic information exchange is viewed in terms of each goal and lists guiding questions and expected outputs, including how eHealth may serve goals beyond the health sector.

Opens Chapter 7 on studying eHealth trends and experience, aiming to learn from other countries' successes and failures and from international good practice. It lists the actions and expected outputs, such as understanding how eHealth is used in similar countries and evidence of its benefits.

Describes researching other countries' eHealth visions, strategies and programmes, listing the information to gather, such as goals, recommendations, changes to information flows, current projects and lessons learned. It advises focusing on countries with similar health systems and goals and using reports from international bodies such as WHO when direct information is lacking.

Recommends interviews, study visits and regional meetings with those responsible for eHealth in countries of interest, focusing on lessons learned. It then describes studying international trends, good practice and outcomes through projects, research and specialist publications, including material from WHO.

Opens Chapter 8 on drafting an unconstrained national eHealth vision that shows how eHealth will help meet national health goals and reflects stakeholder input and global trends. It lists actions, such as agreeing a time frame, defining desired outcomes and drafting the vision, and the expected outputs, including optional scenarios.

Explains how to agree the time frame for the eHealth vision, taking into account the national health strategy, other countries' experience and guidance from senior decision-makers. It then begins describing how to define the desired eHealth outcomes, which derive from strategic goals and the country context and form the basis for identifying required components.

Table 15 offers example questions for defining eHealth outcomes, covering changes needed in health services, such as care models, coordination, workforce, quality and costs. It also covers changes in health information flows, such as sharing patient and population health data and reporting. The text advises deferring wider stakeholder consultation on outcomes until the vision statement and its effect on stakeholder groups are drafted.

Explains how to link each eHealth outcome to the strategic context so that the vision clearly supports health system goals and does not appear irrelevant. A box gives examples linking eHealth outcomes to health system goals, and stakeholder consultation is again advised once the draft vision is ready.

Describes how to write the initial vision statement in plain, non-technical language that policy-makers can endorse and stakeholders can understand. A box gives a template stating that by a given date eHealth will deliver strategic benefits through changes in health information flows.

Advises developing the vision statement in internal working sessions and reviewing it with a small stakeholder group before wider consultation. It then explains how to describe what the vision means for each stakeholder group, using example questions in Table 16 about current difficulties and expected improvements.

A box gives an example eHealth vision for health care providers to 2020, contrasting today's problems, such as incomplete information, duplicated services and manual coordination, with expected improvements. The vision promises better-informed decisions at the point of care, decision-support tools and easier information sharing between providers. The page ends by introducing the development of scenarios showing the vision in practice.

Gives an example scenario of Akeyo, a woman in rural East Africa recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during her daughter's vaccination visit. It describes her current long journeys, rare contact with the same doctor and poor continuity of care. It then shows how eHealth could improve her care and help her avoid serious complications, so she can keep working and caring for her family.

Describes scenario development as a creative storytelling exercise, using examples of eHealth services to add realism, and advises reviewing scenarios with stakeholder groups to improve accuracy and build support.

Opens Chapter 9 on identifying the eHealth components needed to deliver the vision across seven areas: leadership and governance, strategy and investment, services and applications, infrastructure, standards and interoperability, legislation and compliance, and workforce. It notes that a strategic eHealth architecture model may optionally be created.

Describes the leadership and governance components needed to direct and coordinate eHealth at national, state, regional and local levels. Table 17 gives examples, such as programme management, stakeholder engagement and strategic architecture, each with a description. The expected outputs include governance bodies, their roles and responsibilities and the relationships between them.

Advises identifying the preferred governance model through internal discussions and workshops and linking it to existing bodies. It then describes the strategy and investment components needed to build, run and sustain the national eHealth environment, with examples in Table 18 such as strategy and planning bodies and investment mechanisms.

Describes the services and applications components that let people, providers and managers access, use and share health information and support new ways of delivering care. Table 19 gives examples, such as individual electronic health information services, and lists uses of health data for research, programme design and regulation.

Explains that service and application components should be linked to the eHealth outcomes in the draft vision, illustrated in a box using rural health workforce shortages and remote access to care as the example. It then introduces infrastructure components, covering both physical technology and the software platforms that support health information exchange.

Table 20 gives examples of eHealth infrastructure components, such as broadband and mobile network coverage, computing infrastructure at all levels, and identification and authentication services. The text advises linking these components to eHealth outcomes in the draft vision so stakeholders see why they are needed.

A box links infrastructure components, such as broadband and computing capacity, to the outcome of electronic access to care for people in rural and remote areas facing health worker shortages. The page then begins describing standards and interoperability components, listing types of health information, such as referrals, test orders and results, care plans and electronic health records.

Continues the table of standards and interoperability components, including common terminology, messaging standards, secure messaging standards and software certification standards. It begins a box example linking these components to improved HIV/AIDS monitoring and reporting.

Completes the HIV/AIDS example, showing how surveillance services, individual electronic health records and data structure standards support population health monitoring. It then introduces the legislation, policy and compliance components needed to protect the privacy, integrity and security of health information.

Table 22 lists legislative and policy components, including broader government policy within and beyond health, and eHealth-specific rules on the privacy, use and sharing of digital health data. It also covers rules on clinical competence, liability for services such as telemedicine, safety and quality. The page closes by introducing workforce components for both health care workers and the staff who build and support eHealth systems.

Table 23 gives examples of eHealth workforce components, such as eHealth skills for health workers, education and training, accreditation and similar needs for ICT staff. The page then advises producing a model of all the components needed to deliver the national eHealth vision.

Figure 9 shows an example national map of eHealth components, such as patient health records, referrals, medication management, chronic disease management, test ordering, health information portals and monitoring functions. The example is credited to an Australian national eHealth strategy prepared by Deloitte in 2008.

Figure 10 presents a stakeholder perspective model for consumers, describing their wish for more access to and control over personal health information and more involvement in managing care. It lists examples such as online health information, health communities, personal health portals and new channels to providers, citing the same Australian strategy.

Opens Chapter 10 on gathering information about the existing national eHealth environment. Actions cover the seven component areas from governance to workforce, and the output identifies existing or planned components that can be reused or shared, along with gaps to address in the action plan.

Describes how to assess the existing eHealth environment to find components that can be reused and gaps to close, with guiding questions under each heading. The governance questions ask which bodies lead eHealth at each level and whether they can run programmes and engage stakeholders. Investment questions begin with how the health system is funded, and a footnote cites Canada Health Infoway and Australia's NEHTA as examples.

Lists further assessment questions on eHealth investment, such as government funding schemes and failed or halted strategies. It continues with questions on services and applications already in use or being piloted and the problems they address. It also asks about providers and vendors of systems such as practice management and clinical information systems.

Lists assessment questions on infrastructure, such as unique identification of individuals, providers and organisations, uptake of computer systems, existing electronic health record repositories and coverage of data and mobile networks. It continues with questions on standards and interoperability, including any large standards initiatives that failed or stalled.

A page of the Russian edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit listing questions for assessing a country's legislation, regulation and compliance relating to eHealth. The questions cover data protection laws, consent, use and disclosure of personal health information, enforcement, and approval processes for eHealth products.

Lists further questions on regulations for e-commerce such as digital signatures, and on the health workforce's eHealth and ICT skills, certification and training. It notes that information can be gathered from documents, research in public and private sectors and reports by WHO or ITU.

Describes consulting health sector stakeholders, such as health care providers, professional bodies and officials at national to local levels, as a key source of information on the current eHealth environment. It notes that this step gathers information without yet analysing its implications.

Opens Chapter 11 on analysing opportunities, gaps, risks and barriers, which compares the existing eHealth environment with the draft vision. It shows the toolkit's process diagram and lists the expected outputs, such as components that can be reused and those that must be developed.

Explains how to compare existing eHealth components with those required, aiming to identify reuse opportunities, gaps, and risks and barriers. It gives questions on whether existing components can be adapted or scaled up and at what cost.
Gives questions for identifying gaps between required and existing eHealth components, the investment and action needed to close them, and the risks, barriers and mitigation measures involved.
Describes the expected outputs of the gap analysis and the approach, a four-step internal assessment followed by stakeholder consultation to confirm the findings.

Opens Chapter 12 on refining the eHealth vision and developing strategic recommendations, adjusting the initial vision in light of the opportunities and gaps found. It lists the expected outputs, including approval of the vision by decision-makers and its presentation to wider stakeholders.

Explains that countries differ in political will, resources and starting points, so they must prioritise which eHealth components to deliver. Table 24 lists internal and external factors that influence prioritisation, and the approach is described as an iterative cycle of analysis and consultation.

Figure 12 and Table 25 set out the three stages of refining the eHealth vision, from analysing the environment to reviewing outcomes, priorities, timelines, commitments and funding, with example questions and possible results.

Stresses that prioritisation should be flexible and strategic rather than detailed programme planning, which is covered in Part 2. It then describes refining the initial vision internally and having the original stakeholders review the result.

Describes developing high-level strategic recommendations for each of the seven types of eHealth components, each with a reference, rationale, actions, dependencies and risks. Box 10 gives example infrastructure recommendations, starting with a national service for unique health identifiers.

Gives a further example recommendation on encouraging providers to invest in basic computing infrastructure, and explains that recommendations should be developed internally and tested with stakeholders. It then describes approving the final vision and recommendations and presenting them to stakeholders, which may involve broader public consultation.
Notes that some countries may hold public consultation before finalising the vision while others move straight to action planning, which is covered in Part 2.

Annex A gives examples of eHealth drawn from WHO's Global Observatory for eHealth, describing electronic health records and types of telehealth such as store-and-forward and remote monitoring services.
Continues the eHealth examples with interactive telehealth services, telecare for older people and those with special needs, mobile health, and health surveillance and monitoring systems.
Describes practice, patient and clinical management systems and health information systems used to manage care and support health system decisions, citing the Health Metrics Network framework.
Annex B, Table 26, lists examples of eHealth benefits, such as better access to services in rural and remote areas, improved efficiency and quality of care, with sources cited.

Annex C proposes a structure for a national eHealth vision document, noting that the order of sections can vary by audience, from strategic context to the seven component areas and strategic recommendations.

Annex D, Table 27, summarises the toolkit's methodology, beginning with the actions and outputs for gathering data on the current eHealth environment across the seven components and reviewing trends and experience in similar countries.
Continues the methodology summary, covering the steps for developing the initial vision, analysing gaps, refining the vision, and approving and communicating it to stakeholders.
Annex E presents a sample national eHealth component map (Figure 13) covering governance, strategy and investment, and services and applications such as telehealth and mobile health.
The second half of the sample eHealth component map, showing services and applications, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation and workforce elements.

Annex F describes a governance continuum, from fully regulated to free-market models with bureaucratic, market or network governance, and notes that the choice depends on the national context and role of government.
Annex G defines terms used in Part 1 of the toolkit, such as strategic goals and objectives, eHealth outcomes and outcome indicators.
The title page of Part 2 of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, on developing a national eHealth action plan.
A page with no extracted text.
A repeated title page for Part 2 of the toolkit, on developing a national eHealth action plan.
The cataloguing and copyright page of the Russian edition of the toolkit, with WHO and ITU ISBNs and the 2012 copyright and disclaimers.

Explains the purpose of Part 2, which builds on the national eHealth vision from Part 1 to develop a comprehensive action plan. It describes the intended audience, including decision-makers who developed a vision by other methods.
Continues the introduction to Part 2, noting the need for an experienced team and outlining the three parts of the toolkit and the structure of Part 2's chapters and annexes.

The table of contents for Part 2, listing chapters from the action plan model to resource requirements, financial constraints and implementation phases, plus annexes on risks and public–private partnerships.
The list of figures and boxes in Part 2 of the toolkit.
The list of tables in Part 2, covering governance arrangements, stakeholder roles, action lines, resources and examples of risks.
A page with no extracted text.

Introduces the move from vision to action plan, recalling what the approved national eHealth vision describes and explaining that the action plan sets out components, governance, funding and coordination at all levels.

Opens Chapter 1 on the action plan model, which sets out the activities, resources and strategic phases needed to implement the eHealth vision (Figure 2). It notes that resources are analysed carefully during planning.
Explains that action plans are usually split into time-bound strategic phases with their own priorities and results, and points to a suggested plan structure in Annex A.
Opens Chapter 2 with an overview of the method for developing a national eHealth action plan (Figure 3), which begins by identifying the activities needed and grouping them into action lines.

Describes in Russian, within the overview of Part 2 of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, how detailed plans for each line of action are combined into a comprehensive eHealth action plan checked against Part 1 priorities. It also covers defining implementation phases so stakeholders see what each phase should achieve.

Opens Chapter 3 in Russian on organising the process of developing the eHealth action plan, showing the overall sequence of steps. It states the aim of effective management by a core team and the expected result of a robust process supported by stakeholders.

Discusses in Russian the role of senior health sector leadership in overseeing development of the action plan, suggesting a formal launch to secure support. It shows the proposed governance structure with leadership, a core team and stakeholder reference and expert groups.

A Russian-language table of proposed governance bodies for developing the eHealth action plan, giving the functions and membership of health sector leadership, the core team and advisory groups. It notes that the core team will build on results from Part 1.

Lists in Russian the skills the Part 2 core team needs, such as national strategic project management, knowledge of the eHealth vision, programme design, costing and stakeholder engagement. The page ends with the process diagram of steps.

Opens Chapter 4 in Russian on engaging stakeholders while developing the eHealth action plan, with the overall process diagram. Its intended result is broad stakeholder acceptance and support for a pragmatic plan.

Explains in Russian how the government's role, from tight control to more collaborative approaches, shapes how the action plan is developed and how stakeholders are involved, with a table of implications. It then lists health sector stakeholders such as public and private providers and NGOs.

Describes in Russian stakeholders outside the health sector, such as ICT ministries and telecom providers and education and research institutions, who may contribute resources or benefit from eHealth. It begins to group stakeholders by role, such as decision-making bodies.
A Russian-language table of common stakeholder roles in developing the eHealth action plan, describing decision-making bodies, key influencers, customers and subject experts with examples of each.

Describes in Russian how to tailor the engagement approach to each stakeholder group's role and interests, with an example table, and advises keeping consultations to a minimum while considering availability.
A Russian-language table giving an example plan for consulting stakeholder groups at each stage of action plan development, from line-of-action planning to defining implementation phases.

Opens Chapter 5 in Russian on defining eHealth lines of action, with the process diagram. Its expected result is a draft plan for each line of action showing outputs, activities, dependencies, timeframes and risks.

Describes in Russian identifying the main eHealth lines of action that group activities with a shared purpose, presenting four general lines drawn from country experience in a table. It recommends between four and six lines of action in the plan.

Continues in Russian, cautioning against too many lines of action and describing the approach of internal analysis and stakeholder input. It suggests testing the initial lines of action with a small group of stakeholders.

Describes in Russian breaking each strategic recommendation from Part 1 into outputs assigned to lines of action, using the example of a national health identification service. Example outputs include required funding for the service.

Gives Russian-language examples of outputs needed under the lines of action for strategic recommendations such as a national health identifier and a national telemedicine service. It then introduces defining activities with their scope, timing and dependencies.
A Russian-language table of the elements that define eHealth activities, such as scope, duration, dependencies and resource needs, followed by example activities for several lines of action.

Lists in Russian example activities for the change and adoption line of action, such as awareness campaigns, a national eHealth information repository and financial incentive schemes. It stresses supporting adoption in priority areas until it becomes self-sustaining.

Gives in Russian questions for identifying change and adoption activities, such as how an activity affects consumers, providers and managers. It then explains the need to identify dependencies between activities within and across lines of action.
Describes in Russian identifying the key dependencies between activities and the reasons for each, to sequence the work plan, with an example diagram citing a 2008 national eHealth strategy.

Explains in Russian sequencing activities and setting timeframes for each line of action, optionally noting responsible stakeholders. It also covers identifying risks and adjusting work plans to reduce them.
Describes in Russian an optional step of refining the eHealth lines of action, for example when many activities lack a logical fit. It notes this may involve consulting stakeholders.

Opens Chapter 6 in Russian on developing the comprehensive action plan once plans for each line of action exist, with the process diagram. The expected result is a plan adjusted to health system and stakeholder priorities with reduced risks.

Describes in Russian combining line-of-action work plans into a single comprehensive draft plan, taking account of interdependencies across lines and timing. It includes an example diagram citing a 2008 national eHealth strategy.

Describes in Russian the two-stage approach to developing the draft action plan through internal workshops: combining the line-of-action plans and re-sequencing them. It then explains comparing the plan with health system and stakeholder priorities.

Describes in Russian assessing how well the plan matches health system and stakeholder priorities and choosing options to improve the fit. It stresses that consultations help build stakeholder understanding and support for the plan.

Describes in Russian identifying implementation risks at the level of the whole action plan rather than individual lines, with sample questions on scope and feasibility. It notes that stakeholders' experience of past programmes can help.

Describes in Russian refining the action plan to fit strategic priorities, for example by changing the sequence and timing of activities. It notes this is done internally using the options agreed with stakeholders.

Opens Chapter 7 in Russian on determining overall resource requirements for the eHealth action plan, with the process diagram. It also covers the approach to securing resources and a rough estimate of the funding needed.

Describes in Russian identifying the skills and expertise needed to implement the action plan and whether the country has or can obtain them, with a table of aspects to consider. It notes that detailed resource planning comes later at activity level.

Describes in Russian the input of subject experts on skills and resource needs, then the step of identifying national constraints on skills and expertise. It points to statistical agencies and industry bodies as sources of workforce data.
Describes in Russian choosing approaches to securing needed skills, such as recruitment, contracting and partnerships, in a table. It introduces the internal analysis of these options.

A Russian-language table of aspects for choosing how to obtain skills and resources, such as constraints and timeframes. It suggests possibly engaging a specialised organisation if expertise must come from international markets.

Describes in Russian estimating the scale of funding needed for the action plan, listing factors such as resource types, ICT capital and operating costs, and service operation. It notes that both bottom-up and top-down estimation methods can be combined.

From the Russian edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, a figure sets out a proposed approach to estimating eHealth funding requirements, covering resource levels, activity duration, ICT and non-ICT costs and existing programmes. The text contrasts top-down estimation with more detailed but time-consuming bottom-up costing of each action plan activity.

Lists the kinds of information used in bottom-up cost estimates, such as resources, duration, skills sourcing and ICT capital and operating costs. It advises presenting estimates as ranges and clearly stating key assumptions for decision-makers.

Opens Chapter 8 on refining the eHealth action plan to fit the country's financial constraints, outlining its purpose and expected output of an adjusted plan and documented implications for the national eHealth vision.

Section 8.1 explains how to assess the funding likely to be available for the action plan, using a table of funding sources, mechanisms and examples. It suggests learning from other countries' innovative approaches to financing eHealth.

Describes dialogue with decision-making bodies to clarify accessible funding, noting that both health and other government bodies should sponsor eHealth programmes. The expected output is an agreed list of changes making the plan feasible within likely funding.

Section 8.2 sets out, in a table, a stepwise approach to identifying and assessing options for adjusting the action plan to available funds, with questions to consider and interim outputs. It notes consultation with stakeholders on the impact of preferred options on the national eHealth vision and health goals.

Section 8.3 describes revising the action plan according to the preferred option, producing an adjusted national eHealth action plan that fits available resources. It also covers updating the eHealth vision to reflect the changes.
Opens Chapter 9 on defining implementation phases for the eHealth action plan, listing tasks to identify logical phases, key messages for stakeholders and objectives for each phase.

Section 9.1 explains how to define logical implementation phases, each describing strategic focus over a period, illustrated with a figure linking action lines and monitoring timeframes. It lists questions about dependencies and external timing factors such as election and funding cycles.

Section 9.2 describes formulating key messages for each implementation phase that convey its strategic focus to decision-makers and stakeholders, such as visible results and changes. It cites Australia's 2008 national eHealth strategy as an example.

Section 9.3 explains how to set objectives for each implementation phase in terms of improvements experienced by key stakeholder groups as they interact with the health system. It again draws on Australia's national eHealth strategy as an example.
Describes the internal analysis of activities in each phase to determine their outputs and their impact on key stakeholder groups.

Annex A proposes a structure and contents for a national eHealth action plan document for stakeholders, covering context, action lines, governance, resource requirements, skills sourcing and implementation period.

Annex B summarizes, in a table, the methodology for developing the national eHealth action plan, listing each stage with its actions and interim outputs, from setting up the process to defining phases and their objectives.

Annex C shows how the eHealth action lines from Chapter 5 map to the national eHealth component map in Part 1, listing services such as real-time clinical data access, appointment booking, telemedicine and mobile health.

A figure mapping eHealth components, including services and applications, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, workforce and policy, to the governance, foundation, solutions and change and adoption action lines.

Annex D gives examples of activities under the four broad eHealth action lines, starting with governance activities. These include establishing coordination and formalizing links with health system governance functions.

Describes foundation activities that build the components needed for secure electronic health information exchange across regions and sectors, giving examples such as national identifiers, terminology standards and infrastructure.

Continues the foundation examples with a national legal framework for protecting health information, then introduces solution activities that deliver eHealth services and applications using the foundation components.

Table 19 lists example solution activities, such as a national investment fund for eHealth solutions, priority applications and identifying health managers ready to adopt and spread eHealth solutions.

Lists example change and adoption activities, including eHealth awareness campaigns, workforce education and engaging clinical and consumer groups to explore issues and risks in the national eHealth environment.

Annex E presents examples of risks associated with eHealth action plan activities, beginning with strategic and stakeholder risks, such as outcomes failing to meet the expectations of political, health and other stakeholders.

Continues the examples of eHealth risks, covering resources and funding and technical and vendor issues, such as vendors not offering products compatible with the national eHealth environment when needed.

Annex F explains public–private partnerships, defining them as collaborations to design, finance, build or operate projects traditionally run by the public sector, and outlines reasons for using them. The references include Australian and Indian sources, with some citation text left in Spanish.

Describes models of public–private partnership, such as build-operate-transfer and build-lease-transfer, and distinguishes PPP as a financing mechanism from other forms of private sector involvement in eHealth.
Annex G defines terms used in the eHealth strategy toolkit, organized by part, from strategic health goals in Part 1 through action plan terms to outcome indicators.

Describes the purpose of Part 3 of the toolkit, which guides countries in building a model for monitoring the action plan and evaluating its results through indicators, targets and governance. It notes the intended audience and shows how Part 3 relates to Parts 1 and 2.
Gives an overview of Part 3's contents, from the introduction linking Part 2 outputs to monitoring, through chapters on the monitoring and evaluation model and detailed guidance, to the annexes.

The table of contents of Part 3, listing chapters on the eHealth monitoring and evaluation model, indicators, baselines and targets, and governance, plus annexes on results-based management, example strategies and definitions.

The list of figures and tables (in Russian) for Part 3 of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, on monitoring and evaluation, covering topics such as results-based management, indicators, baselines and targets, and governance of national monitoring.

Introduces Part 3 of the toolkit (in Russian), noting that by this stage a government should have an approved national eHealth vision and action plan with action lines, outputs, timelines, resources and phases. It explains that monitoring and evaluation track and assess the plan's results using a results-based management chain, shown in a figure; a footnote citation is in Spanish.

Distinguishes monitoring and evaluation of the eHealth strategy from programme management, which tracks inputs, activities and outputs to check whether implementation is on track (in Russian). It explains that monitoring and evaluation complement this by measuring outcomes and impact; footnotes cite project management sources in Spanish.

Stresses that building a national monitoring and evaluation framework needs dedicated resources and should be budgeted within national eHealth programmes, with countries encouraged to use the results chain concepts (in Russian).

Chapter 1 (in Russian) describes the elements of an eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework: indicators, baselines and targets, and governance and processes, shown in a figure. It explains the two types of indicators, output indicators on adoption of eHealth and outcome indicators on the results achieved.
Explains the need for baselines and time-bound targets to track the action plan and for national governance to oversee monitoring and evaluation and respond to deviations (in Russian).

Chapter 2 (in Russian) gives an overview of the sequential method for developing the monitoring and evaluation framework: defining indicators, setting baselines and targets, and defining governance. It stresses consulting stakeholders and aligning indicators with other health reporting timelines.

Continues the overview (in Russian), describing setting baselines and targets for several time periods and defining governance and processes so that monitoring at different levels sits within a single national framework.

Chapter 3 (in Russian) introduces defining eHealth indicators, aiming to identify output and outcome indicators linked to the stakeholders and outcomes from Part 1. It lists the steps, starting with identifying priority stakeholders, and the expected outputs.

Describes identifying priority stakeholders inside and outside the health sector to whom eHealth results must be demonstrated, defined by organization or role rather than individuals (in Russian). It then explains describing what each eHealth outcome will mean for each stakeholder.

Gives a figure linking stakeholders, eHealth outcomes and indicators, and a table of example outcomes by stakeholder (in Russian). Examples include better primary care access for rural consumers, help for pregnant women in remote areas and wider access to evidence for researchers.

Explains reviewing the eHealth outcomes defined in Part 1 and making them specific enough to measure for each stakeholder (in Russian). It then introduces identifying the eHealth outputs that contribute to those outcomes, with footnotes referring back to Part 1.

A table (in Russian) of example eHealth outputs linked to outcomes for stakeholders, such as connectivity in rural communities, a national telemedicine service and computer access infrastructure. It notes that some outputs are achieved gradually and others at a point in time.

Describes reviewing and agreeing priority outputs and outcomes with key stakeholders, since limited resources mean not everything can be measured (in Russian). It explains that output indicators measure adoption and outcome indicators measure the resulting improvements, which are closely linked.

Gives a figure showing how output and outcome indicators relate and explains that output indicators suit outputs achieved in stages, such as infrastructure rollout (in Russian). Example indicators include increased use of a national provider information portal and provider satisfaction.

A table (in Russian) of example outcome and output indicators for health managers and administrators, such as reduced time to detect and respond to outbreaks and support for health workforce education. It also includes indicators for consumers on telemedicine awareness and satisfaction.

A table (in Russian) of example outcome and output indicators for health care providers, such as more electronic exchanges of health information, less time spent obtaining patient histories and provider satisfaction. It also covers e-learning participation by the health workforce.

Discusses using quantitative and qualitative indicators, with qualitative measures from surveys and feedback helping explain deviations from expected results (in Russian). It describes an internal analysis to identify candidate indicators for agreement with stakeholders and the need for skills in both types of analysis.

Chapter 4 (in Russian) introduces setting baselines and targets for each indicator, with time frames for measurement against targets. It explains that baselines show the starting point and help set realistic targets for assessing progress.

Describes setting national timeframes for monitoring and evaluation, which help governments see whether the plan is achieving results, spot problems and keep stakeholders informed (in Russian). It suggests aligning with implementation phases while considering stakeholder reporting requirements.

Lists further factors for monitoring timeframes, such as political and funding cycles and the pace of eHealth implementation (in Russian). It then describes establishing a baseline for each indicator and notes that many countries may first need to build data collection capacity.

Describes setting realistic, achievable targets for each output indicator over time, before outcome targets that depend on them (in Russian). It refers to an illustrative table of output targets and lists questions to consider, such as the baseline and timeframe.

Lists further questions for setting output targets, such as other concurrent activities, external research and links between indicators, and the implementation targets from the action plan (in Russian). It then introduces setting ambitious but realistic targets for outcome indicators.

A table (in Russian) of example outcome indicator targets at 3, 6 and 10 years, such as the share of primary care consultations by telemedicine. It explains that outcome targets are set through internal analysis and reviewed with experts and stakeholders.
Chapter 5 (in Russian) introduces defining the governance model and processes that bring together all actors for national eHealth monitoring and evaluation, listing its activities and outputs.

Describes defining a national governance model for eHealth monitoring and evaluation, which coordinates the various actors and differs from programme management (in Russian). A table of governance functions begins, including national analysis and evaluation by a cross-sector coordinating body.

Continues the table of governance functions (in Russian), covering expert support from the health ministry, NGOs and international organizations such as WHO and ITU, and research capacity. It recommends a dedicated national monitoring and evaluation body that gives the programme steering committee an independent view.

Explains that the national monitoring body may be a new or existing agency or a contracted service, and that individual and external eHealth projects monitor themselves within the national framework (in Russian). A table sets out the roles of governance mechanisms, from health sector leadership to cross-sector stakeholders who help assess targets and corrective action.

Continues the table of governance roles (in Russian), covering eHealth project teams and external projects that set aligned indicators, monitor them and report to the national body. It advises using existing governance mechanisms where possible and clarifying each one's responsibilities.

Describes defining the national monitoring and evaluation process, a continuous cycle alongside implementation in which each indicator is assessed at agreed times (in Russian). It notes that activity-level processes should align with the national framework and that designing a pragmatic process is hard for large programmes.

A table (in Russian) of example monitoring and evaluation actions at national and activity level across planning and initiation, data collection, analysis and reporting. It ends with reviewing and adjusting unrealistic targets and agreeing revised targets for later periods.

Chapter 6 (in Russian) concludes that the toolkit guides countries in developing an eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework, which will need updating as national contexts change. It stresses regular reporting on progress and results to maintain transparency and stakeholder support.

Annex A (in Russian) introduces results-based management, increasingly important for the UN and its agencies, which shifts the focus from processes to performance and outcomes. A figure shows the logical framework from inputs and activities to outputs, outcomes and goals.

Explains that results-based management plans top-down from goals to inputs and manages bottom-up from inputs to results, with a table of the concepts (in Russian). It then defines monitoring and evaluation and their relationship to the results chain.

Gives a figure relating monitoring and evaluation to the results chain, showing that monitoring tracks implementation while evaluation measures the changes and impact achieved (in Russian). It lists what effective monitoring and evaluation require, from defining expected results to collecting data, drawing conclusions and making recommendations.

Continues the table of example national eHealth strategies, listing documents from Mauritius, Saudi Arabia, Scotland, the United States and others with links and publication dates.

Annex C defines the terms used in the toolkit, organized by toolkit part. Terms include strategic goals and challenges for eHealth, components of the national vision and outcome indicators for stakeholders.
